source.text: וְ/נִינְוֵ֥ה כִ/בְרֵֽכַת מַ֖יִם מִ֣/ימֵי הִ֑יא וְ/הֵ֣מָּה נָסִ֔ים עִמְד֥וּ עֲמֹ֖דוּ וְ/אֵ֥ין מַפְנֶֽה־׃

translation.text: Nineveh has been like a pool of water from her earliest days[b], yet they are fleeing. “Stop! Stop!”[a]—but no one turns back.

footnotes.text: Or “Stand! Stand!” The Hebrew imperatives can be rendered more literally this way; “Stop! Stop!” brings out the sense in a flight scene.

POB provisionally reads the phrase as ‘from her days.’ The selected Greek has ‘her waters,’ an alternative interpretation of the pool imagery. Published 4Q82 preserves the unpointed spelling מימיה, but its following context is supplied; the spelling can also be read temporally. Source priority remains uncertain.

lexical_decisions.rationale: Proper place name; transliterated per translation philosophy.
The simile compares Nineveh to a collected body of water. 'Pool' is natural English and preserves the image without over-specifying an engineered reservoir.

alternatives: from the days she has existed
from the days of her being
lexical_decisions.rationale: The present pointed Masoretic text is provisionally interpreted temporally. The selected Greek has ‘her waters’; published 4Q82 preserves מימיה, but its unpointed spelling permits temporal and water analyses and the following context is supplied. The water alternative involves source interpretation, not simply an English synonym of the pointed base. Source priority remains unresolved; the retained main wording is not certified optimal.

The pronoun plus participle describes flight. Under POB's provisionally retained temporal reading, the pronoun refers to Nineveh's people and ‘yet’ expresses a contrast with its earlier condition. The water interpretation of the preceding phrase requires its own syntax and referent assessment; this note application does not decide it.

alternatives: Hold your ground! Hold your ground!
lexical_decisions.rationale: Imperative repetition heightens urgency. In this context of fleeing troops/citizens, English 'Stop! Stop!' best conveys the shouted command to halt, while 'stand' is preserved as an alternative.

The Hiphil participial form from פנה here denotes turning oneself around/back in response to the command. Rendering it personally ('no one turns back') fits the scene better than an abstract noun phrase.
